questiontext.text:
Here is a proof of the same kind as the example above. Its last step is missing.

Statement: the sum of any {@words@} is a multiple of {@mfac@}.

Proof. Let the {@words@} be {@nums@}, where \(k\) is an integer. Their sum is {@sumw@} \(= {@sumexp@}\).

[The last step is missing.]

Hence the sum of any {@words@} is a multiple of {@mfac@}.

(a) Complete the factorisation.

\({@sumexp@} = {@mfac@}\,\big(\) [[input:ans1]] \(\big)\) [[validation:ans1]]
[[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Which fact shows that this is a multiple of {@mfac@}?

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]
[[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Here is the whole proof.

Let the {@words@} be {@nums@}, where \(k\) is an integer. Their sum is {@sumw@} \(= {@sumexp@} = {@mfac@}({@ta1@})\). Since \(k\) is an integer, \({@ta1@}\) is an integer, so the sum is {@mfac@} times an integer: a multiple of {@mfac@}. Hence the sum of any {@words@} is a multiple of {@mfac@}.

This is the method of the example: write the numbers in terms of \(k\), simplify, take out the factor, and say why what is left is an integer. The reason is that the bracket is an integer. It need not be even or positive, and the numbers being added need not have the factor themselves: with \(k = 0\) they are {@zerow@}.

[[if test="is(vF = 5)"]]

The sum \(8k + 12\) is a multiple of 4 but not always of 8: for \(k = 1\) it is 20.

[[/if]]

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 6.1 (the sum of any two consecutive odd numbers is a multiple of 4), p. 24, in Section 6 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

node.description: Factor times bracket gives the sum

truefeedback.text: Check by expanding: \({@mfac@}({@dslip@}) = {@expand(mfac*dslip)@}\), not \({@sumexp@}\). Every term must be divided by {@mfac@}, the constant term too.

node.description: Diagnostic: the whole sum in the bracket

truefeedback.text: That is the whole sum. The bracket is what you multiply {@mfac@} by to get the sum.

falsefeedback.text: Divide each term of \({@sumexp@}\) by {@mfac@}, then check by expanding \({@mfac@}(\ldots)\).

truefeedback.text: Yes: since \(k\) is an integer, the bracket is an integer, and {@mfac@} times an integer is a multiple of {@mfac@}, by definition.

node.description: Diagnostic: the bracket must be even

truefeedback.text: The bracket need not be even: \({@mfac@} \times 3 = {@3*mfac@}\) is a multiple of {@mfac@}. Go back to the definition of a multiple of {@mfac@}.

node.description: Diagnostic: each number has the factor

truefeedback.text: The numbers being added need not have the factor: with \(k = 0\) they are {@zerow@}, and not all of these are multiples of {@mfac@}. Only their sum is.

falsefeedback.text: Negative numbers can be multiples too: \(-{@mfac@} = {@mfac@} \times (-1)\). For negative \(k\) the bracket is negative, and the sum is still a multiple of {@mfac@}. Go back to the definition of a multiple of {@mfac@}: what must the bracket be?
